column2: The alphabet's first animal and Africa's 'earth pig'; eats fifty thousand ants a night and never once says thank you.
A fluffy cousin of the llama, farmed for the softest jumpers; as the joke goes, it will happily pack your suitcase — 'I'll…'.
A South American giant that subdues dinner by squeezing; chewing is for amateurs.
A little tank in a leathery coat that jumps straight up when startled; terrific against coyotes, hopeless against cars.
A handy word for any fleet, elegant herbivore; essentially 'deer, but with a better agent'.
A stripy-faced digger with the temper of a tiny landlord; brooks no nonsense, foxes included.
The savannah's sprinter: nought to sixty in three seconds flat; everything after that is coasting.
A lizard that changes colour and swivels each eye independently; can watch you and judge you in two directions at once.
A river veteran unchanged since the dinosaurs; one specimen developed a taste for captains and a lifelong fear of ticking clocks.
A tiny rodent famous for falling asleep mid-tea-party in Wonderland; lifestyle goals, frankly.
Pink from a diet of shrimp and able to sleep standing on one leg; an achievement yogis have chased for centuries.
An antelope so elegant that 'graceful' is contractually required before its name; lions find it delicious, which seems ungrateful.
The ceiling-walking lizard with Velcro toes; also, allegedly, sells you car insurance.
A burrowing rodent that treats lawns and golf greens as personal construction sites; the groundskeeper's tiniest nemesis.
A bear that can outrun a horse yet mostly chooses salmon and berries; admire it from a very long lens.
A patient grey fisherman standing on one leg; has mastered the art of doing nothing until lunch swims by.
The only bird that flies backwards, on a heart of 1,200 beats a minute; runs on nectar and pure nerves.
An antelope that leaps three metres straight up, as if the savannah were a surprise trampoline; also a vintage Chevrolet.
A resourceful wild dog with a taste for leftovers; its howl is contractually obliged to appear in every night scene ever filmed.
Sleeps twenty hours a day on a diet of mildly toxic leaves; proof that you can have it all and still nap.
A small arctic rodent unfairly accused of cliff-diving en masse; the myth was staged by a 1958 film crew, which is the real scandal.
A woolly pack animal with firm opinions and expert aim when it spits; highland drama on four legs.
A tufted-eared wild cat with the stare of a creature that has already judged you and found you wanting.
The desert's sentinel, standing guard while everyone else digs; 'simples', as a certain advert taught a nation.
The unicorn of the sea, its eight-foot tusk actually an overgrown tooth; dentistry has questions.
A spotted wild cat of compact size and twice the glamour; Salvador Dali walked one around town on a leash, naturally.
A forest giraffe in zebra-striped stockings; nature kept the first draft and called it a masterpiece.
The red-haired ape with the jungle's most judgmental stare; strictly arboreal and thoroughly unimpressed.
The river's acrobat, holding hands while asleep so as not to drift apart; setting a standard the rest of us cannot meet.
An armour-plated mammal rolled into a pinecone; the world's most trafficked animal and, visually, a walking artichoke.
A duck-billed, egg-laying, venomous mammal with webbed feet; when nature couldn't decide, it simply said yes to everything.
A rodent carrying some thirty thousand quills and zero patience; love, here, genuinely hurts.
A sea parrot in clown makeup that mates for life; months alone on the ocean, and it still beats your flight home.
A bird whose bill is half its body and all of its brand identity; can reach both the fruit and the cereal box.
The great lion of Narnia — not a tame lion, and never safe, as he politely warns; winter tends to end where he walks.
A diminutive Gaul holding off an entire empire with a magic potion and a winged helmet; the Romans regret everything.
Lawyer Finch of Maycomb, who defends the innocent for free and sets the standard for fictional fathers everywhere.
A hobbit who leaves home without a pocket-handkerchief, burgles a dragon, and returns just in time for his own auction.
The castaway who ran a desert island like a spreadsheet for twenty-eight years; made goatskin umbrellas briefly fashionable.
France's greatest swordsman and nose, ghost-writing love letters for a handsomer man; romance's most generous loser.
The Mother of Dragons, whose titles take a full minute to recite; do not come between her and her children.
The house-elf a sock set free; a free elf, always — and the only character whose exit everyone agreed came too soon.
The man whose portrait ages while he stays flawless; the original filter, with the personality to match.
Shakespeare's enormous knight, devoted to sack, fibs and tavern credit; the greatest character never to settle a bar tab.
An orange cat whose philosophy fits on a T-shirt: coffee, lasagne, and a principled refusal to acknowledge Mondays.
Master Finn, lighting out for the Territory rather than be civilised; rafted the great river with a friend and a disputed conscience.
The alter ego who appears after dark, once the doctor has taken his little tincture; every Victorian gentleman's warning label.
An elven archer with immaculate hair who surfs down stairs shooting orcs; treats dwarf banter as light cardio.
The title character of the Scottish Play — actors dare not say more; ambitious, badly advised by witches, awkward at dinners.
Dahl's tiny bookworm with telekinesis and parents who deserve her; proves a library card is a weapon of justice.
Kipling's man-cub, raised by wolves and fluent in jungle; the original feral heart-throb, minus the paperwork.
The menhir-carrier who fell into the magic potion as a baby; permanently superhuman and permanently on a diet, by decree.
A snowman who dreams of summer and warm hugs; living proof that optimism ignores thermodynamics.
A Very Small Animal with a Very Large capacity for worry; brave precisely because he is frightened, which is the whole point.
The little Belgian detective with the magnificent moustache and the little grey cells; insists on Belgium, never France.
A bear of Very Little Brain and considerable appetite; a cautionary tale about getting stuck in doorways for honey.
Practically perfect in every way, and she has measured it; arrives with the east wind and never explains the carpet bag.
The heroine with the world's most demanding haircare routine; lets her hair down, and the prince's insurance premiums go up.
Panza, squire to the Knight of the Sad Countenance; brings the donkey, the snacks and every ounce of common sense in the book.
A Great Dane solving mysteries on a payment plan of sandwiches; hides from ghosts behind the softest available furnishing.
The potions master of shifting allegiance and a doe-shaped patronus; 'Always.'
A beagle novelist and WWI flying ace, working from the roof of a red doghouse; the novel opens 'It was a dark and stormy night' and stalls there.
The boy reporter with the quiff, forever rescued by a small white dog; accompanied by two bowler-hatted twins in unrelated mishaps.
The little Lannister who drinks and knows things; the sharpest tongue in Westeros and, periodically, its only adult.
The Dark Lord, everyone's father, breathing like a kettle on its last legs; committed to the black wardrobe and never looked back.
The storytelling girl who flew to Neverland and spent the trip mothering the lost boys; bring your own thimble.
The reclusive chocolatier with the golden tickets and the questionable safety record; the Oompa-Loompas run the HR department.
Australia's city of churches, cheerful and modestly overlooked beside its bigger siblings; locals file that under 'bliss'.
The Indian city of the Taj Mahal; a marble monument to love, and to a very patient workforce.
The Texas capital that resolved to stay weird and largely succeeded; music, barbecue, and a million bats commuting at dusk.
Thailand's capital, holder of the world's longest ceremonial name; locals sensibly stick to the short version.
The Northern Irish capital where the Titanic was built — 'she was fine when we left her'; now famous for cranes, murals and giant causes.
An Atlantic island famed for a triangle that eats ships and shorts that end scandalously early; the suntan, at least, is real.
The American city where a tea party gave an empire a migraine; now marathons, colleges and a municipal shortage of the letter R.
Queensland's sunny capital on a lazy brown river; Australia's 'third city' and entirely at peace with the title.
Greece's largest island, home of the Minotaur, his labyrinth and a diet your doctor keeps approving; archaeologists arrive yearly and refuse to leave.
The Mile-High City, and there is a step on the Capitol to prove it; the air is thin and the gold-rush ghosts are comfortable.
Scotland's castle-crowned capital; each August it triples in population with comedians and people politely pretending they got the joke.
At 8,849 metres, the roof of the world, climbed 'because it is there'; the summit queue now requires reservations.
Ecuador's islands where the wildlife never learned to fear humans; Darwin's open-air notebook, giant tortoises included.
Scotland's biggest city, shipbuilder on the Clyde and world capital of warm insults; the accent doubles as encryption.
The school of witchcraft reached from platform nine-and-three-quarters; exams include turning a rat into a goblet and surviving certain teachers.
Hawaii's capital, where history at Pearl Harbor and the surf share the same sun; the lei at the airport is optional but recommended.
The 'mighty' New York river; Henry went looking for China, found fog, and stayed for the real estate.
The Himalayan valley of saffron fields and goats producing famously soft wool; also a Led Zeppelin track nobody can dance to.
The English port of the Beatles, two rival cathedrals and an anthem nobody escapes; around here, you never walk alone — it's the law.
France's longest river, its banks lined with chateaux as if the aristocracy were holding a beauty contest; the wine judges are lenient.
The English city of rain, football and the factory that started the modern world; the rain is described locally as 'character-building'.
The kingdom at the back of the wardrobe; always winter and never Christmas — until a certain lion turns up.
The Canadian province containing Toronto and a Great Lake of the same name; 'beautiful water' in the local First Nations' tongue, and the licence plates concur.
Canada's capital, chosen at a distance by Queen Victoria in what locals suspect was a coin toss; in winter, the world's longest skating rink runs past parliament.
The canal country whose world-famous hat is actually from Ecuador; a logistics triumph wearing someone else's headwear.
Australia's most isolated capital — closer to Jakarta than to Sydney; residents regard the distance as a feature, not a bug.
The Greek island of the Colossus, which probably never straddled the harbour, but let's not spoil it; one of the Seven Wonders, now rather shorter.
The great North American range where the deer and the antelope play, reportedly rent-free; scenery on an unreasonable scale.
The Greek island of white houses, blue domes and sunsets that make proposals statistically more likely; a volcano with superb public relations.
The drizzly home of grunge, a coffee empire and a Needle that appears whenever the fog permits; umbrellas are for tourists.
The Canadian city where you can ski, sail and be rained on in a single afternoon; Hollywood's stand-in whenever New York is over budget.
The Croatian capital, home of the Museum of Broken Relationships — busy since opening day; coffee here is a civic institution.
The Swiss city of banks and discreet wealth; legend placed gnomes guarding the vaults, and no one has confirmed they ever left.
